p: Yes.

there's new appointments that had to be made for that um, Committee that meets, um, which we participate in. Yeah, I mean, it's a huge program to plan for, so hopefully—

Yes, but we're, you know, I mean, any opportunity I think that we have to build, um, solar or any other, um, uh, infrastructure for, um, reducing our emissions is obviously an exciting opportunity for us.

Okay. Now, the hottest summer days are not here, but when they do arrive, the Energy Demand Management Program, which reduces pollution, reduces energy costs, and saves public agencies obviously money on the hottest days, uh, the data shows that DCAS has energy savings and revenue generated by the program have plateaued in recent years. So my question is, do you have the resources

to expand this successful energy demand management program? But particularly in the summer, obviously.

I am, yup.
Yeah.
I mean, how's it going basically is what I'm trying to say.

Um, revenue, yes.
Too much revenue.
Revenue, yep.

been a lifetime since we last interacted when I was at

Um, so just really quickly, um, in terms of the Space Savings Initiative, um, throughout various plans we have seen several adjustments to account for various space savings initiatives, and, uh, they aim to make better use of the city's owned and leased spaces to reduce costs. And just wanted to know how much did the city save from space savings initiatives in FY25, and how much has been saved to date in FY26?

I just want to note, um, on the space savings, uh, obviously there's been a tremendous amount of work that has b-been done to survey all all of the agencies, and that's one of the things that I'm really excited to dig into because I think there's a lot of potential there. But, um, we have already started to do some of that work, so I'll, I'll give it to, uh, the First Deputy Commissioner to sort of add the numbers here.

Thank you, Commissioner. Um, so Fiscal Year '25 was a big planning year, um, getting the surveys out, identifying, um, agency space usage

needs. Um, in Fiscal Year '26, um, year to date, we've already realized almost $8 million, and that's a combination of cost avoidance as well as actual savings to the lease budget.
Perfect and, um, do you keep a record of which agencies, uh, are sharing spaces? And is this publicly reported anywhere that we can access?
Um, we'll have our DC of— our EDC of real estate and facilities management.

Good morning. Thank you for that question. So it's not currently publicly reported except that our— all of our lease data is available, uh, online and, and that is publicly reported. So you would be able to, you know, eventually see, uh, lease reductions where we're vacating a space entirely. Uh, but some examples are, um, the Law Department consolidated some of its space at 100 Church Street and we were able to move the Campaign Finance Board out of another lease site into that site, thereby relinquishing space at 80 Main and Lane. Um, another example is HRA consolidating out of, uh, 404 Pine or Department of Finance, um, consolidating into one of

their other sites so HRO could move into their vacated site. So that's just some examples of how we got to those numbers.
Perfect. Um, and how do you determine which agencies would be best suited to share space? Is there some kind of survey or—
Um, we persuade them nicely.
I'm sorry?
We persuade them nicely. I mean, I mean, it really works.

Well, I was just gonna say, I mean, I think the general process as we're sort of, um, as people's leases come up and stuff like that, we look at a case-by-case basis and what the agency's needs are, and we, um, think about like where we can actually put them. And at that point, you know, because there's a little bit of a moving target as we're sort of doing each of these moves because, um, you know, the space, the space evolves as people- as you know, from being in an agency, the space evolves as people sort of have moved from one space to another.

So we're constantly refining and having conversations with the agencies about their needs, and then we'll figure out where we can fit people. But our number one goal, obviously, is to make sure that we're being responsible with the taxpayer dollars and, um, you know, also making sure that agencies have adequate space to work in.
Perfect, thank you. Um, and just moving on to Con Edison Smart Charge and other adjustments I say this as someone who drives an EV car, full EV, and selfishly I have a question because-
I want to— she wants a charging station at City Hall Park.

No, but you know what's crazy is that I asked if I could charge here and I was told no because I'm technically not a city vehicle, but I would gladly pay if I was like in some kind of emergency situation. So I'm just wondering if we're allowed to charge at City Hall.
She’s been asking this since the day she started.
Yeah, exactly.

I will just say, um, we are very aggressively expanding our charging infrastructure. And in fact, one of the things that I like to, um, brag about early and often is that DCAS is— has the largest, uh, charging infrastructure in the state. Um, and, uh, er, along with DOT. Um, and, um, we are constantly looking for places to install, um, charging, not just for city fleet, but we also are now, um, starting to install public, um, charging places. Um, so we are very eager if you have any sites in your district that you think might be a viable option, obviously tell us.
One at City Hall.
Yes, I'll let, I'll let Keith speak to that specific location.

Yeah, and just to add really quickly, I can recommend places because we're a transit desert in Eastern Queens, and so there's no trains or subways or Long Island Railroads. And so this is something that the community would love.

That would be great. Yeah, and I mean, I think the— obviously there, there are certain criteria that you have to sort of look for in terms of like the electric grid, um, and that's something

that we work closely with Con Ed on. But, um, I don't know, Keith, if you wanted to add anything.

Sure. So the first, the good news, we have a workplace charging initiative. City Hall is in it. We can work out right after this meeting for you to charge. You will have to pay because it is your personal car. But that done, we will have you set up before the end of the day or as soon as we are in touch with you. And then, yeah, we are very open to ideas about additional charging. You know, finding space is the challenge for us. We are in the field every single day with Con Ed assessing locations. If it's viable at a logistics level, right, you gotta have access. And of course, there's got to have juice. We have to have available electric but if you provide us with lists, we can be out there, you know, very soon and in assessing those locations.

Perfect um, and then just more going to the budget piece of this, uh, the Smart Charge. I know the Preliminary Plan includes an additional $1.2 million in other categorical funding for FY26. Only for incentive revenue received for the city's participation in the program. And so how does

Con Ed determine the incentive funding and what types of services and activities are considered?
Keith, you're their most popular guest star.
Yes.

Uh, hmm, so Con Ed has been a really important partner for us and they have the Smart Charge, but then the Ready Charge is actually the big one for us. And so they are providing for every one of the electric chargers that we're installing and just for background, we run the largest, like, fast charging electric network in New York State. We have 415 fast chargers. We are installing more fast chargers literally every single week. So they're providing an offset based not on the pedestal, not on the unit, but based on the electrical upgrades or the electrical costs and those are extraordinarily important funds for us, and we are using those to reinvest uh, that's actually how we do Level 2 chargers. So the slow charger, the overnight charger, most of that is funded through Con Ed grants.

It's also how consistent with Local Law 140, we train mechanics and city fleet operators, um, to really learn about EV and understand how to operate and maintain EV. So the Con Ed partnership has been very important and it really is a daily thing. We are in the field with Con Ed today and every day. And, and what— are there any limitations in terms of how you can utilize the funds once they come back?

I don't believe there is a limitation. I do believe it comes in as general purpose, um, grant funding because it is an offset to expenditures but the reality is how we do in fact use it is to reinvest in our sustainability program. Right. Um, and have you assessed ways to increase participation in the program by city agencies to increase the incentive revenues from Con Ed?
So on the smart charge, yes. So we do have a smart charge program. It involves incentivizing you for basically off-peak charging.
Uhm, mmm.

And so we do that with all our non-emergency agencies where we can. Right? So there are some agencies, you know, I, I, I can't restrict

the charging of police electric cars and other emergency response vehicles. We have to give them flexibility. But certainly, say, at the Parks Department and DEP where you can charge overnight, we are doing that and we are bringing in a revenue stream. As you noted, we are bringing in that smart charge revenue, revenue stream.

Okay and I just have one quick question Chair, if that's okay, on Local Law 97. Um, only because this is a law that really impacts my district heavily because I, despite what people may think, I actually have the most number of co-ops and condos in my area. And so I bring this up to say that there's a bill— there's a couple bills we have that are sort of making adjustments. I know it's probably different for you all because you're, um, city buildings, but, um, the— based on what I'm understanding, the Governor and the State Comptroller themselves have come out with reports basically saying that the grid's not going to be ready in time. And so we're trying to figure out a way, um, at least on the constituency side and the residential side, how to not have the penalties be exorbitant?

Because I know in 2030, um, that's really when the higher fines are going to start and so, if there's a bill in place that we have that literally just matches, uh, the penalties and fees to when the grid will actually be ready, um, is that something that would be helpful, or is it something that would—

I think from, uh, DCAS's perspective You know, we, I think, feel not only are we mandated, but we have a moral obligation to, to move as fast as we can on this. Um, and as, um, uh, you know, as I was sort of referring to earlier when we were doing Q&A, we do have, um, this large source of hydropower that's coming online soon, which will actually allow DCAS to, um, to allow the city to, to meet the targets. So, um, uh, and exceed, I, I should say. And, and also we are very aggressively working on all of the these projects to reduce our consumption. So I don't think that, um, I think for, for, for us, um, even, you know, mandates aside, we want to do as much as possible.

Hmm, mmm, no and I totally get that and I think it's just challenging for— I, I get, and it's good that on the city side you feel

very confident that you can meet those goals. I think the other issue just goes on beyond the, you know, city buildings and where we land with that. So I just wanted to get your thoughts on that, but that's good to hear. So thank you.
Thank you.
Thank you, Chair.
Thank you very much. Uh, Council Member Hankerson.

Thank you, Chair. Uh, I just have a couple of questions, um, regarding some of the recruitment strategies, um, that DCAS uses. Uh, what is DCAS doing to attract more applicants for city jobs? If I can start there.

Thank you, Council Member. Um, so this is something that I'm very excited to dig into because I think, um, there's a, there's a lot of strategies that we already do, and then there's more that I think that we can do. But, um, one of the things I'll just say, and then I'll pass it to our Deputy Commissioner, um, to talk, um, in greater detail about the programs that we do have, is sort of even just demystifying what the civil service system is.

Um, 80% of our, um, jobs are civil service jobs. And I think if you ask a normal New Yorker, they probably couldn't tell you what civil service is. Um, so, you know, I think we're having, you know, conversations with, um, the team, uh, including our comms team about, you know, how can we sort of explain to New Yorkers what civil service is and make sure that when tests are posted, um, that, uh, that people actually know about it and not just people who, you know, would normally know about it, but also broader parts of New Yorkers, especially our graduating high school students and our graduating college students. Um, so we just, um, uh, cut a TikTok video— not TikTok video, Instagram video, sorry— with, um, our DEP commissioner, for example, um, to promote one of our, um, engineering, um, intern exams, um, which will be, uh, which, which will hopefully, you know, help us reach sort of a broader audience. So things like that but I'm gonna pass it to Deputy Commissioner Porter because we also have a number of, um, you know, um, ah, Public Service Corps programs and such that, um, also specifically target, um, broader populations.

Sure, thank you for the question. Um, so first and foremost, we work hand in hand with city agencies to develop our annual examination schedule. Um, as Commissioner mentioned, 83% of the positions used across city government require a civil service list. Uh, so we work very closely with agencies to ensure that their hiring needs are, um, met through the, the civil service process. In addition to that, uh, our workforce operations team at DCAS, which consists of, um, uh, the, uh, Pathway Programs team, uh, the Public Service Corp team, as, um, Commissioner mentioned, they work hand in hand to use data to drive, you know, the areas that we visit for, um, available hiring events, and also, um, working closely with the New York City Public School to, um, uh, educate our youth about, uh, available civil service exams. There are also a number of local laws that help to drive how we recruit, um, for the City of New York. Um, so there are many different ways that we do so, but the ma— major driver is Civil Service Exam.

I appreciate that and I know, uh, that you mentioned Instagram, uh, which kind of leads or segways to my next question. Um,

what's the agency's means of marketing and how much of your budget is allocated toward marketing efforts?

So, um, we have, uh, in addition to all of the work that we do, um, in our, um, you know, public affairs team, which I think from a budget standpoint might be difficult to sort of separate out because it's sort of all intertwined. We also have an office of recruitment within human capital. Um, but I'll, um, I'll hand it to you to add any numbers.

That's right, Commissioner. Um, the marketing budget is intertwined. Um, but our Office of Recruitment, which sits under Human Capital, they have a budget of about $500,000, and they have— they're a small but mighty team, 6 of them. They go out to, um, uh, college events. They do Civil Service 101 presentations across the city. Um, and, um, we— they, they were instrumental when DCAS did the hiring halls. They were supporting agencies across the city in those events.

And if I can just sort of shamelessly, um, plug, uh, we're— we are actually currently hiring for a director of digital content,

um, uh, in order to sort of help drive some of this, um, more social media oriented strategy.
Oh, that's great, okay.
So if you have any good candidates, please send them our way.

Will do. Um, I know in, in the, the last, uh, Administration, Uh, there was an initiative that, um, required DCAS, uh, to host job fairs citywide. Uh, how many individuals were hired as a result of those, uh, job fairs?
Um, sorry, go ahead.

Um, so we can get back to you with the number. Um, but the hiring halls that DCAS participated in were back in, uh, 2023. That process has now transitioned to the Small Business Services, and they hold— host, um, hiring pool— hiring halls, um, with both public and, uh, private sector employers. Uh, DCAS's role, um, in that process is to, um, connect city agencies with these events, um, to recruit for city jobs.
That's my time. Thank you.
Thank you.

I have one more question.
Go right ahead.

Um, er, I don't know if you have the data for this, but going back to the initial— the original hiring halls, um, do you know which agencies seen an increase, uh, in terms of hiring as a result of those hiring halls? KATRINA PORTER So we saw major success with hiring halls across the board. Um, I think it would be more helpful for us to get back to you since this— that, uh, particular event happened some time ago. I don't wanna misrepresent.
Thank you so much.
Yeah.

Oh, thank you. Um, did you get any state money? 'Cause I know the Proposed Executive Budget in January came out. Now we're waiting for the— One House bills to be negotiated, but were there any state good or bad opportunities in that budget? What did you think?
Yeah, so there were some, um, positive impacts in the, um, the budget, which, um, I think we have here that we can, we can go into. I think a lot around vehicles, for example.
Mostly around policy, um, climate policy that we're always supportive of.
Okay.

Um, the state removed the cap on rebates. Provided to municipalities for clean vehicle infrastructure, which I'm sure Keith is very happy about. Um, they're also extend— they're— the Governor's Budget is proposing to extend the alternative fuels exemption for 5 years. Um, so we're always happy to see, um, more state policy going towards helping us achieve our climate goals.
Well, that's good. Okay, so basically it wasn't money per se, but it is in the end.
Yes.

Okay um, emergency oil purchase. The plan preliminary includes an additional $3.0 million in intra-city funds for FY26 only for heating oil for, from the Department of Education. I

guess it's, you know, it's called some other name now, something about public schools. How was this amount determined? Does this funding relate to the warming centers that were operating at those DOE facilities during the snowstorms? Do you manage all energy-related expenditures for DOE? And if so, why are they managed by— why by DCAS and not DOE? And what portion is covered by DCAS and what portion by DOE? Um, the reason I ask this is it is complicated for those of us on the outside to know because you are so integrated.
Yes.
Other agencies. Um, how does this all work? So how does the oil and DOE and you work?

So, yeah, so, um, this was obviously a very historic winter. Um, in terms of the amount of snowfall and the, the many days of, of, uh, extreme cold. Um, so we were, um, called in to help. Um, and, uh, there's an emergency, um, fleet emergency fuel task force which we helped, um, coordinate. Um, and, uh, it's, it's sort of— so I guess the short answer is it is sort of like an, an

additive, um, effort, um, on our part to sort of come in and sort of help them supplement their fuel. Um, but, uh, Keith, do you wanna add anything to that?

Sure, on a day-to-day basis, um, New York City Public Schools has their own version of the DCAS fuel contract that they actually manage day-to-day. So on a day-to-day basis, we are not managing your fuel deliveries because of the extreme cold temperatures. There was really a, you know, an enormous amount of demand on heating oil. There was also in the broader marketplace, but also impacting city government, a dearth of available drivers. There's law that mandates how your drivers have to have rest periods. And, you know, our vendors were searching far and wide, getting drivers from other states. But, and so we came in to manage through our emergency contract with this, which is actually not with the day-to-day vendor.
Okay.

An emergency trucking operation to support the public schools. So Sanitation, um, DCAS, the fire department, the police department, the

Department of Transportation, all using their city trucks to make sure that heating oil got delivered to the schools, um, during really about a, a week to 10-day period when it was just incredibly cold and, and we wanted to make sure there were no problems.
Okay, so that basically that was your effort during that time period.

Well, it's a, it's a coordinating effort. So like, for example, shout out to Department of Transportation, who in particular gave us a lot of drivers for this effort. Um, so we coordinate other agencies to do it. So I don't want to steal their thunder, but I will say, like all things DCAS, quietly, very dramatic behind the scenes.
And there was a cost, obviously, in addition to your usual budget. Do you have some numbers for that?
Yes, um, because it was an emergency, the cost was estimated around $300,000 a day.
Okay.

Um, we didn't— at the time, we didn't know how long it could have been, so we estimated assuming we would need to do it for about

10 days. The actual cost came in a little lower, about a little over $1 million. So we intend to give some of that— give the rest of the money back to DOE. So you may see that reversed in the next budget cycle.

Okay, thank you. Um, the Preliminary Plan includes an additional $1.9 million in this Intracity funds for FY26, only for— from the DOE for Geotab equipment. So what kinds of vehicles, DOE vehicles, are the Geotab equipment used for? What are the metrics for tracking them? What's done with the data? And are all of DOE's vehicles equipped? And if the Geotab equipment, is it used on school buses for tracking? Now we all know that the school bus issue is challenging on all fronts since I get so many complaints. So, I know you're working on this, and so I just want to understand it for the parents and for the public.

Okay, thank you. So all of New York State Public Schools city-owned vehicles, about 300 or so, are tracked through our Fleet Office of Real-Time Tracking, which is Geotab. That's funded

through DCAS. Um, but then DCAS also tracks a little bit more than 10,000 school buses live. So there is a local law that requires tracking, as you know, that was passed a number of years ago during— after a major sudden storm. The tracking for the school buses does happen through the Fleet Office of Real-Time Tracking, um, with all the companies. We provide all of that information on a daily basis, and of course live access to New York City Public Schools, to the Office of Pupil Transportation. Each company also has access to their information.
You mean each company, each busing company?
Each busing company also has access to their information, so they can be mon— and we are monitoring safety, utilization, idling, and, and many other—
Times, delivery times.

All kinds of indicators, right? You know, the data is very robust. Um, the actual management of the school buses is still, of course, the Office of Pupil Transportation. We're really the

telematics support service but we also develop a lot of, uh, reporting for them.

And what do you do with that data? The reason I ask, of course, is that unfortunately, uh, you don't get the accolades for doing a great job. Everybody thinks this is all DOE, just so you know, in terms of this program. So my question is, what— did the DOE use the data to try to improve? Is that the idea?

Yeah, I mean, absolutely and we, you know, in the end, the Office of Pupil Transportation and the Department of Education, these are all contracted services through the Department of Education, not through DCAS. So ultimately, it, it, you know, it's their charge, not DCAS's, to manage the school bus operation but we are supporting them on a daily basis, providing safety reports, utilization reports, helping them analytically wherever they ask us to.
Okay, and it's your impression that all of the school buses are equipped?
All of them are equipped.
Okay.
And I, I will just add, um, I think it would be fun to have, um, any Council Members here who are interested come see the Fort where we do our, um, fleet coordination as well.

I would, I would like to do that. I think the bus contract is like 2.5 years. It's shorter than it has been in the past. So we'll see how this data, uh, helps with any future decisions about school buses. My, my disabled students often don't get there on time. So I have a lot of concerns. Um, I think the city secured a federal grant to help purchase electric buses, but have these funds have been slow to be dispersed? I didn't know the funding, uh, went to DCAS or to DOE and if you have any update about purchasing these electric school buses.
It goes to the
It goes to the DOE. So they're, they're the ones who are purchasing the very slow, er, not slow buses, but slow arriving Federal money, they're dealing with it, not you.
Yes, yes.

Okay, that's lucky for you, I would say. Um, uh, a couple of things. Hmm, goal 80

times 50, there's a carbon reduction goal to reduce 80% of our overall emissions, and I think you're, you know, doing a, a great job, um, by 2050 using 2006 as a baseline for our city. So do you feel that the 2006 baseline is a good measure and have you assessed whether it can meet this mandate? The carbon reduction.
I'm not, um, I'm not sure that we, um, have any objection to the 2006 baseline, but, um, I don't know if you—
But do you feel like you can meet the mandate? I think that's a more important question.
